desc: Trace block device I/O and print details incl. issuing PID.
r: biosnoop - Trace block device I/O and print details incl. issuing PID.

This tools traces block device I/O (disk I/O), and prints a one-line summary for each I/O showing various details. These include the latency from the time of issue to the device to its completion, and the PID and process name from when the I/O was first created (which usually identifies the responsible process).

This uses in-kernel eBPF maps to cache process details (PID and comm) by I/O request, as well as a starting timestamp for calculating I/O latency.

This works by tracing various kernel blk_*() functions using dynamic tracing, and will need updating to match any changes to these functions.

This makes use of a Linux 4.4 feature (bpf_perf_event_output()); for kernels older than 4.4, see the version under tools/old, which uses an older mechanism

Since this uses BPF, only the root user can use this tool.

<dl><dt data-o="">-h</dt><dd>Print usage message.</dd><dt data-o="">-Q</dt><dd>Include a column showing the time spent queued in the OS.</dd><dt data-o="">-d DISK</dt><dd>Trace this disk only.</dd><dt data-o="">-P</dt><dd>Display block I/O pattern (sequential or random).</dd></dl>

Trace all block device I/O and print a summary line per I/O:
# biosnoop

<dl><dt>TIME(s)</dt><dd>Time of the I/O completion, in seconds since the first I/O was seen.</dd><dt>COMM</dt><dd>Cached process name, if present. This usually (but isn't guaranteed) to identify the responsible process for the I/O.</dd><dt>PID</dt><dd>Cached process ID, if present. This usually (but isn't guaranteed) to identify the responsible process for the I/O.</dd><dt>DISK</dt><dd>Disk device name.</dd><dt>T</dt><dd>Type of I/O: R = read, W = write. This is a simplification.</dd><dt>SECTOR</dt><dd>Device sector for the I/O.</dd><dt>BYTES</dt><dd>Size of the I/O, in bytes.</dd><dt>QUE(ms)</dt><dd>Time the I/O was queued in the OS before being issued to the device, in milliseconds.</dd><dt>LAT(ms)</dt><dd>Time for the I/O (latency) from the issue to the device, to its completion, in milliseconds.</dd></dl>
Since block device I/O usually has a relatively low frequency (< 10,000/s), the overhead for this tool is expected to be negligible. For high IOPS storage systems, test and quantify before use.

This is from bcc.

https://github.com/iovisor/bcc
